content:
Are they nstmp files or folders? I find discussion of both.

They are temporary files that are created while folders are compacted, then are normally deleted when the compaction is complete. You can safely delete the oldest ones. I would keep a few of the newest ones.

Your real concern shouldn't be what they are, but why are they left there? I don't have any, and if they're created during a compaction, they must disappear so quickly I never see them. Most mentions of them I find are almost 20 years old, so it seems to not be a common Thunderbird effect. I find some mentions that leftover nstmp files can be caused by certain operating system indexing utilities. the one most mentioned being Google Desktop. Do you use anything like that?

I think I read that they can be left if you quit Thunderbird while a compaction is still going on. When you start it again later, the compaction is supposed to resume. But unless you were to have a long-time bad habit of doing that a lot, I don't think that adequately explains it.

Without any specific evidence, I would tend to blame your anti-virus program, if you use one. They are notorious for grabbing hold of files and not letting them go so the file can't be properly written to disk. If you find these popping up again, you can try temporarily disabling your AV or creating a scanning exception for your Thunderbird Profile folder.

content:
There's a slight possibility you can recover the messages on the notebook using the unofficial add-on "Undelete", available here:

https://www.ggbs.de/extensions/Undelete.html

The conditions have to be right. To quote the web page,

This add-on allows you to restore accidentally deleted messages under certain conditions. The following requirements must be met:

- It must be an IMAP, POP3 or local folder.

- It cannot be a synthetic folder such as saved searches or unified folders.

- The message storage type must be 'File per folder (mbox)' (but this is the default). For an IMAP folder, this must also apply to the 'Local Folders'.

- With IMAP, the folder must be 'selected for offline use' (but this is the default).

- The folder must not be compacted.

I don't know if this will work on the desktop PC when the messages were deleted on another computer, but its worth a try.

content:
Once you have changed a password by logging on to your webmail account using a browser, you can then update the stored password in Thunderbird.

In Thunderbird

  • Settings > Privacy & Security
  • Passwords section
  • click on 'Saved Passwords'
  • click on 'Show Passwords'

Each mail account will have two lines for incoming and smtp

  • right click on each line and select 'Edit Password'
  • completely clear contents and then carefully type in the updated correct password.
  • click on 'Close'

(NOTE: the above does not apply if using Oauth, when there should be only one line containing the oauth token) If account uses Oauth as Authentication Method and you want to renew password and reset Oauth. You would need to delete the stored Oauth line and any other stored password for the account. After a restart, you will get prompted in a browser to enter the updated password and allow Thunderbird access to server at which point a new oauth token will get created and stored automatically.

Exit Thunderbird Allow a dew moments for background processes to complete, then restart Thunderbird.
